timeline.name: Spanish-American War
timeline.desc: Congress declared war on Spain in April 1898; fighting in Cuba and the Philippines ended with the August 12, 1898 armistice, and the Treaty of Paris followed in December 1898.

timeline.name: Philippine-American War
timeline.desc: U.S. forces fought Filipino independence forces after the United States acquired the Philippines from Spain; President Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed the conflict over on July 4, 1902, though fighting continued in some areas.

timeline.name: World War I (U.S. involvement)
timeline.desc: The United States declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917 and fought until the Armistice of November 11, 1918.

timeline.name: World War II (U.S. involvement)
timeline.desc: After the December 7, 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, the United States declared war on Japan, Germany and Italy, and fought until Japan formally surrendered on September 2, 1945.

timeline.name: Cold War (era band)
timeline.desc: A U.S.-Soviet geopolitical rivalry, conventionally dated from the March 1947 Truman Doctrine to the December 1991 dissolution of the Soviet Union, marked by an arms race and proxy conflicts rather than direct war between the two powers.

timeline.name: Cold War event: Truman Doctrine
timeline.desc: President Truman asked Congress in March 1947 for aid to Greece and Turkey, establishing a policy of containing Soviet influence.

timeline.name: Cold War event: Berlin Airlift
timeline.desc: The United States and its allies supplied West Berlin by air after the Soviet Union blockaded land access from June 1948 to May 1949.

timeline.name: Cold War event: NATO founded
timeline.desc: The North Atlantic Treaty, signed in April 1949, created a collective-defense alliance of the United States, Canada and Western European states.

timeline.name: Cold War event: Sputnik
timeline.desc: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in October 1957, intensifying the U.S.-Soviet space and missile competition.

timeline.name: Cold War event: Cuban Missile Crisis
timeline.short: Cold War event: Cuban Missile Crisis
timeline.desc: In October 1962 the United States and the Soviet Union confronted each other over Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, ending with the missiles' withdrawal.

timeline.name: Cold War event: Berlin Wall opens
timeline.short: Cold War event: Berlin Wall opens
timeline.desc: East Germany opened the Berlin Wall in November 1989 amid the collapse of communist governments in Eastern Europe.

timeline.name: Cold War event: Soviet Union dissolves
timeline.short: Cold War event: Soviet Union dissolves
timeline.desc: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, conventionally marking the end of the Cold War.

timeline.name: Korean War
timeline.desc: After North Korea invaded South Korea on June 25, 1950, U.S. forces fought under a UN Security Council-authorized command, without a declaration of war, until the armistice of July 27, 1953.

timeline.name: Vietnam War
timeline.desc: After the August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incidents Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, and U.S. combat forces fought in Vietnam until the January 1973 Paris Peace Accords; Saigon fell in April 1975.

timeline.name: Lebanon multinational force
timeline.desc: U.S. Marines deployed to Beirut as part of a multinational force; after the October 1983 bombing of the Marine barracks, the force withdrew in February 1984.

timeline.name: Grenada (Operation Urgent Fury)
timeline.desc: U.S. forces landed in Grenada on October 25, 1983 after a coup, citing the safety of U.S. citizens, and combat forces withdrew by mid-December 1983.

timeline.name: Panama (Operation Just Cause)
timeline.desc: U.S. forces invaded Panama on December 20, 1989 and removed Manuel Noriega from power; he surrendered to U.S. forces on January 3, 1990.

timeline.name: Persian Gulf War (Desert Shield/Desert Storm)
timeline.desc: After Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990, a U.S.-led coalition deployed to the region and, under UN Security Council Resolution 678 and a January 1991 congressional authorization, expelled Iraqi forces, with a ceasefire on February 28, 1991.

timeline.name: Bosnia air campaign (Operation Deliberate Force)
timeline.desc: NATO aircraft, including U.S. forces, struck Bosnian Serb military targets in August-September 1995, ahead of the Dayton peace agreement.

timeline.name: Kosovo air campaign (Operation Allied Force)
timeline.desc: NATO, including U.S. forces, conducted an air campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia over Kosovo from March 24 to June 10, 1999.

timeline.name: Global War on Terrorism (2001 AUMF era)
timeline.short: Global War on Terrorism (2001 AUMF era)
timeline.desc: After the September 11, 2001 attacks Congress passed the 2001 AUMF, which successive administrations have cited as legal authority for counterterrorism operations in several countries.

timeline.name: Afghanistan War
timeline.desc: U.S. forces began operations in Afghanistan on October 7, 2001 against al-Qaeda and the Taliban government, and the last U.S. forces withdrew on August 30, 2021.

timeline.name: Iraq War
timeline.desc: U.S.-led forces invaded Iraq on March 20, 2003 under the 2002 Iraq AUMF and removed Saddam Hussein's government; U.S. forces remained through a long counterinsurgency until withdrawing in December 2011.

timeline.name: Libya (Operation Odyssey Dawn / NATO)
timeline.desc: Under UN Security Council Resolution 1973, U.S. forces led the initial air and missile strikes on Libyan government forces beginning March 19, 2011, before NATO took command; operations ended in October 2011.

timeline.name: Anti-ISIS campaign (Operation Inherent Resolve)
timeline.desc: U.S. forces began air strikes against the Islamic State in Iraq in August 2014 and in Syria in September 2014; end date left blank because the mission's current status was not verified for this file.

timeline.name: U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear sites (Operation Midnight Hammer)
timeline.short: U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear sites (Operation Midnight Hammer)
timeline.desc: On June 21, 2025 (U.S. Eastern time), U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear facilities at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan during the June 13-24 Israel-Iran war; Iran fired missiles at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar on June 23, and a ceasefire took effect June 24.

timeline.name: U.S.-Iran conflict, 2026
timeline.desc: U.S. and Israeli forces began strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 without a congressional declaration or authorization; an April 7-8 ceasefire was followed by a U.S. naval blockade, intermittent exchanges and renewed U.S. strikes in June-July, and no ceasefire or settlement was in force as of October 8, 2026.

majors.name: World War I (U.S. involvement)
majors.legal_basis: Declarations of war on Germany (Apr 6 1917) and Austria-Hungary (Dec 7 1917)
majors.description: The United States declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917 and fought until the Armistice of November 11, 1918.
majors.era_note: Classical gold standard at $20.67/oz with a wartime gold-export embargo (Sept 1917 - June 1919); the new Federal Reserve (opened 1914) lent to banks against war bonds; financed by Liberty Loans plus a big income-tax expansion.
majors.one_liner: Debt grew about twentyfold, mostly through Liberty Loans, and prices rose about 17–18% a year in 1917 and 1918.

majors.name: World War II (U.S. involvement)
majors.legal_basis: Declarations of war on Japan (Dec 8 1941) and Germany and Italy (Dec 11 1941)
majors.description: After the December 7, 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, the United States declared war on Japan, Germany and Italy, and fought until Japan formally surrendered on September 2, 1945.
majors.era_note: Gold Reserve Act regime ($35/oz, no domestic gold convertibility); from 1942 the Fed pegged T-bill yields at 3/8% and capped long Treasury yields at about 2.5% (yield-curve control) until the March 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord; price controls and rationing.
majors.one_liner: Defense took 37% of the economy at its 1944 peak. Debt held by the public passed 100% of GDP and the money supply more than doubled while the Fed capped interest rates.

majors.name: Korean War
majors.legal_basis: UN Security Council resolutions (June-July 1950); no declaration or AUMF
majors.description: After North Korea invaded South Korea on June 25, 1950, U.S. forces fought under a UN Security Council-authorized command, without a declaration of war, until the armistice of July 27, 1953.
majors.era_note: Bretton Woods ($35/oz for foreign central banks); the March 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord ended the wartime rate peg in the middle of the war; tax increases (Revenue Acts of 1950-51) covered much of the cost.
majors.one_liner: Paid for mostly with taxes: debt rose only 7% while defense nearly tripled as a share of GDP. Inflation spiked to 7.9% in 1951.

majors.name: Vietnam War
majors.legal_basis: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, P.L. 88-408 (Aug 10 1964); repealed 1971
majors.description: After the August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incidents Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, and U.S. combat forces fought in Vietnam until the January 1973 Paris Peace Accords; Saigon fell in April 1975.
majors.era_note: "Guns and butter": war plus Great Society spending under Bretton Woods; rising inflation and gold outflows ended with Nixon closing the gold window on Aug 15, 1971, so the war ended in the early fiat era.
majors.one_liner: Guns and butter: the money supply more than doubled while debt rose 48%. Inflation built up and peaked at 11% in 1974, after the 1971 gold-window closing.

majors.name: Persian Gulf War (Desert Shield/Desert Storm)
majors.legal_basis: UN Security Council Resolution 678 and AUMF P.L. 102-1 (Jan 14 1991)
majors.description: After Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990, a U.S.-led coalition deployed to the region and, under UN Security Council Resolution 678 and a January 1991 congressional authorization, expelled Iraqi forces, with a ceasefire on February 28, 1991.
majors.era_note: Fiat / floating-dollar era; short war during the 1990-91 recession.
majors.one_liner: A short war mostly paid for by allies (CRS: $61B cost, $4.7B net to U.S. taxpayers). Debt rose $730B over the same window for other reasons, the 1990–91 recession among them.
majors.crs_note: CRS: most Gulf War costs were offset by allied contributions or absorbed by DoD; net cost to U.S. taxpayers $4.7bn (current $).

majors.name: Iraq War
majors.description: U.S.-led forces invaded Iraq on March 20, 2003 under the 2002 Iraq AUMF and removed Saddam Hussein's government; U.S. forces remained through a long counterinsurgency until withdrawing in December 2011.
majors.era_note: Fiat era; financed mainly by borrowing and emergency/war supplemental appropriations; the 2008 financial crisis and the first rounds of Fed QE happened mid-war.
majors.one_liner: Fought with borrowed money in the fiat era: debt held by the public went from 33% to 70% of GDP. CRS counts $715B of war costs through 2010; the rest of the $9.85T reflects everything else, including the 2008 crisis.

majors.name: U.S.-Iran conflict, 2026
majors.legal_basis: No declaration or AUMF; presidential authority with War Powers Resolution reports to Congress; war-powers resolutions to end hostilities have failed to become law
majors.description: U.S. and Israeli forces began strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 without a congressional declaration or authorization; an April 7-8 ceasefire was followed by a U.S. naval blockade, intermittent exchanges and renewed U.S. strikes in June-July, and no ceasefire or settlement was in force as of October 8, 2026.
majors.status: ongoing, intermittent; White House asserted on May 1 that hostilities had "terminated", but fighting resumed in June-July; no ceasefire in force
majors.era_note: Fiat era; began with gross federal debt above 120% of GDP and a Fed balance sheet of roughly $6.6 trillion (see data); conflict ongoing, so all "war" numbers are year-to-date.
majors.one_liner: U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran began on Feb 28, 2026, without a declaration of war or congressional authorization. The conflict is ongoing and intermittent, so every figure here is 2026 year-to-date.
majors.crs_cost_years: Feb-May 2026 (DoD operational estimate, per CRS IN12678)

closing: Big wars were paid for mostly with borrowing and new money. Korea was the exception: it was paid for mostly with taxes.
